title: Who sets the order wins
hook: Same three voters, same rankings. Change only the order of the votes.

knows: a vote between two options goes to the one with more votes
doesNotKnow: that majority preferences can go in a circle, so the order of the votes decides the winner

misconception: If a group prefers A to B and B to C, it prefers A to C; the group has a clear favourite, and the order of the votes cannot change it.
objective: The learner can explain that with these three rankings each option beats one rival and loses to another by 2 to 1, so the option held to the last vote wins and whoever sets the agenda picks the winner.

claims.text: With the rankings A>B>C, B>C>A and C>A>B, A beats B, B beats C and C beats A, each by 2 votes to 1.
claims.source: Pairwise count in node: A over B for voters 1 and 3; B over C for voters 1 and 2; C over A for voters 2 and 3. The stage prints each tally.
claims.address: stage (vote lines, arrows) and reveal paragraph 2

claims.text: If every voter votes for the option they rank higher, the agenda 'A vs B, then C' elects C, 'B vs C, then A' elects A and 'A vs C, then B' elects B, so the option held back to the last vote wins.
claims.source: Node run of the exact rule used in Demo.tsx (two-way majority, winner meets the held-back option) over all six agenda orders: each of A, B, C wins twice, always the one held to the last vote.
claims.address: hook, prediction (answer C), stage vote lines, reveal paragraph 1

claims.text: Because each option loses 2 to 1 to another, no option beats every other in a pairwise vote, so there is no majority favourite and whoever sets the order of the votes picks the winner.
claims.source: Follows from c1 and c2. A cycle of majority preferences is the topic of Easley & Kleinberg 2010, ch. 23 section 23.3 (section number unconfirmed; fact-checker to confirm against the book). No name or date is used in learner text.

claims.text: This holds when every voter backs the option they rank higher in each vote (sincere voting). The lesson does not claim that real elections have such cycles.
claims.source: Modelling assumption stated in the reveal; the brief excludes any claim about real elections.

recall.question: Three friends rank films: Ana P>Q>R, Ben Q>R>P, Cy R>P>Q. Everyone votes for the film they rank higher. They vote Q against R, then the winner against P. Which film wins?
recall.why: Q beats R 2 to 1 (Ana, Ben), then P beats Q 2 to 1 (Ana, Cy). The film held to the last vote wins, because the rankings form a cycle.
